newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court to hear federal gun law arguments.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court to hear federal gun law arguments.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday hears a constitutional challenge to the Brady Act, a 1993 gun-control law that launched the first congressional effort to regulate firearms in a quarter-century.

In a case that could affect the reach of federal power over the states, the justices will consider during the hour-long arguments whether Congress exceeded its power in adopting the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act.
The law was named after former former White House Press Secretary James Brady, who was shot in the head and partially paralysed in the 1981 assassination attempt on President Ronald Reagan.

President Bill Clinton signed the bill into law after congressional passage marked by a fierce battle between gun control advocates led by Brady and his wife Sarah on the one side and the National Rifle Association on the other.

The law requires a five-day waiting period before the sale of a handgun. During that time local sheriffs must check on whether the prospective buyer has a felony record, a history of mental illness or drug use or other problems that would bar the sale.
It was the first gun-control measure passed by Congress since 1968. A ban on certain types of assault weapons has since been approved as well.
The local background checks were intended as an interim measure until a national computerized system becomes fully operational in late 1998.
But Montana Sheriff Jay Printz and Arizona Sheriff Richard Mack have sued, charging that Congress exceeded its power to direct local law enforcement officials in their duties.
They said the law violates the Constitution's 10th Amendment, which protects state and local governments from certain federal interference.
At the White House, Clinton told reporters on the eve of the court challenge that he believes the Brady law passes constitutional muster.

"We have clearly preserved the right to keep and bear arms consistent with the Constitution, but we have also made America a safer place," he said. "There are tens of thousands of people with criminal backgrounds and other serious problems who couldn't get handguns because of the Brady law.
"People are alive today because of it. It's a better country because of it."
A top administration lawyer also defended the measure.

Acting Solicitor General Walter Dellinger, the government's chief advocate before the Supreme Court, said Congress responded to a national epidemic of handgun violence in adopting a law that requires "interim, limited and nonpolicymaking participation" by local officials.

"The federal government has not compelled the states to enact into law a regulatory regime, nor has it foisted on the states the obligation to solve a controversial policy issue," Dellinger said in a 51-page argument filed with the court.

"The Brady Act advances values of federalism by temporarily placing the record-check function in the hands of local officials, who are most likely to know the community where the proposed firearm transfer is to occur."
The case, due to be decided before July, gives the Supreme Court another opportunity to limit congressional power over the states.

In 1995, the high court struck down a federal law that bars possession of firearms near schools on the grounds that Congress exceeded its power to regulate under the Constitution's interstate commerce clause.
It followed up with a decision in 1996 that Congress may not take away a state's immunity from lawsuit.
